raw_text:
Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) is an infiltrative cardiomyopathy caused by extracellular deposition of misfolded protein fibrils in the myocardium. More than 30 amyloidogenic proteins are recognized, but clinically important CA is dominated by immunoglobulin light-chain amyloidosis (AL) and transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTR), the latter occurring as variant/hereditary (ATTRv) or wild-type disease (ATTRwt) [1-4]. Although historically considered rare and untreatable, CA is now an increasingly recognized cause of heart failure, arrhythmia, and conduction disease because of better awareness, bone-tracer scintigraphy, cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR), and disease-modifying therapies [5,6]. ATTRwt is particularly relevant in older adults: it has been detected in a meaningful minority of patients hospitalized with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and in older patients with severe aortic stenosis undergoing transcatheter valve replacement [7,8]. Musculoskeletal “red flags,” especially bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, lumbar spinal stenosis, and biceps tendon rupture, may precede cardiac diagnosis by years [9].

The clinical phenotype reflects restrictive physiology, impaired longitudinal systolic function, autonomic dysfunction, atrial myopathy, and conduction-system infiltration. Patients commonly present with exertional dyspnea, edema, orthostatic hypotension, intolerance of beta-blockers or renin–angiotensin blockade, atrial fibrillation, low-flow/low-gradient aortic stenosis, or discordance between increased ventricular wall thickness and low QRS voltage. Prognosis varies by amyloid type and disease stage. In AL, circulating cardiotoxic light chains plus myocardial deposition can produce rapid deterioration; cardiac biomarkers are central to staging [10,11]. Very advanced cardiac AL, particularly with high NT-proBNP and hypotension, carries substantial early mortality despite therapy [12,13].

Diagnosis requires both confirmation of amyloid cardiomyopathy and accurate amyloid typing. Tissue biopsy with Congo red staining remains definitive, and mass-spectrometry proteomics is the preferred method when typing is uncertain or immunohistochemistry is equivocal [14]. However, ATTR-CM can often be diagnosed without biopsy: grade 2–3 myocardial uptake on technetium-labeled bone scintigraphy, combined with absence of a monoclonal protein by serum free light chains plus serum and urine immunofixation, has very high specificity [15-17]. This caveat is critical because AL may show tracer uptake and requires urgent hematologic treatment. Echocardiography raises suspicion through increased wall thickness, diastolic dysfunction, biatrial enlargement, pericardial effusion, valve thickening, and reduced global longitudinal strain with relative apical sparing [18]. CMR provides complementary tissue characterization; native T1 and extracellular volume are elevated, and diffuse subendocardial or transmural late gadolinium enhancement has diagnostic and prognostic value [19,20].

Management is multidisciplinary and combines supportive heart-failure care with amyloid-specific treatment. Loop diuretics, sodium restriction, careful volume assessment, treatment of atrial arrhythmias, anticoagulation when atrial fibrillation is present, and pacing for clinically significant conduction disease are central; conventional neurohormonal therapies are often poorly tolerated. In AL, the therapeutic priority is rapid suppression of the plasma-cell clone. Hematologic and cardiac responses are monitored using free light chains and NT-proBNP-based criteria [21]. Bortezomib-based cyclophosphamide–bortezomib–dexamethasone became a common frontline regimen [22], and the ANDROMEDA trial established daratumumab plus cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone as a highly effective standard for newly diagnosed systemic AL amyloidosis, improving deep hematologic responses and organ responses [23]. Selected patients may undergo autologous stem-cell transplantation, but advanced cardiac involvement often limits eligibility.

For ATTR-CM, treatment targets the transthyretin pathway. Tafamidis, a kinetic stabilizer of the TTR tetramer, reduced mortality, cardiovascular hospitalization, and decline in function and quality of life in ATTR-ACT [24], with extension data supporting long-term survival benefit and emphasizing earlier treatment [25]. Acoramidis, another TTR stabilizer, improved a hierarchical composite of mortality, cardiovascular hospitalization, NT-proBNP, and 6-minute walk distance in ATTRibute-CM [26]. TTR gene-silencing therapies reduce hepatic TTR production. Patisiran improved neuropathy in hereditary ATTR amyloidosis [27] and showed favorable cardiac signals in a prespecified cardiac subgroup [28]; in APOLLO-B it preserved functional capacity and health status in ATTR-CM [29]. Vutrisiran, administered subcutaneously every 12 weeks, reduced the composite of death and recurrent cardiovascular events and slowed decline in 6-minute walk distance and health status in HELIOS-B [30].

The field is moving from late recognition to proactive case-finding among high-risk phenotypes and earlier disease-modifying therapy. Remaining priorities include equitable screening, better staging beyond biomarkers, optimal sequencing or combination of stabilizers and silencers, management of advanced disease, and integration of patient-centered outcomes into long-term care.
